I have read The Boys at least...4 different times? I have the Vol 1. in my closet, the big one with the thick cover too. I honestly was excited at the fact that the idea of The Boys was going to get its time to shine in live action media. The comic definitely helped me understand just how much of a fantasy world DC and Marvel had created. I was a bit weary at first, I thought that Hughie being American was a bit of an odd choice, but I was ready for it because I had read up on the casting. Then they showed his dad and it's Simon Pegg, once I saw that I knew that this show was going to be a fucking treat and it didn't fail to deliver. Listen, I'm the first person to defend the comics for what they are, which is an amazing piece of visual media that shows what an actual world with superheroes would be like, but the comic is also 13 years old, we live in a way different world now, so the changes make sense. Karl Urban as Butcher honestly sells it to me, this is not the Butcher who we see in the comics that's always in control, and that makes him a lot more human. The fact that his motivations are still the same honestly redeems the character. The first major change in plot is the fact that Raynor and Butcher are not sleeping together, therefore Butcher has no leverage against her. It changes the plot immensely, and I for one, love it. I like Comics Butcher a lot, but this Butcher feels more real. Frenchie being a jack of all trades instead of a maniac with a taste for violence also made sense. Frenchie in the comics was there for a lot of comedic relief, past the violence and blood he was honestly a silly character. Now he's not silly anymore, at least not as much. He embodies the Frenchie from the Comics in that he listens to his intuitions and he's a very sensitive person, and again that makes sense. His relationship with The Female (Kimiko) is going to be important going forward. This is another big plot change, but I think it makes sense to avoid unnecessary flashbacks. Us comic readers know how it ends, and for me the changes they made to that relationship and the plot behind it make it that much better. Mother's Milk is still the same levelheaded, calculating guy from the Comics. He seems to be missing his powers from the Comics, but I think we should hold off on that judgement for now. The man ran into a barrage of bullets and came back clean. I think this hints at him having some sort of power and will be explored next season. Finally, Hughie. Oh man Hughie. Hughie in the Comics is the readers eyes, he is thrown into this world just like the reader is, without a fucking clue. Show Hughie is the same, but whereas Comics Hughie was honestly not that useful when he got into the team (which comic readers find out later why he was even sought out by Butcher to begin with), Show Hughie is very useful in an age filled with technology. His meeting with Butcher and the reason he gets contacted makes sense. His character progression through all 8 episodes makes sense, and the fact that he even has doubts up until the 6th episode shows very strong writing. Not a single minute, a single second, a single action was wasted in this show. Everything about it makes sense, everything just clicks. The Boys don't get away with everything without consequence, the Supes have legitimate reasons for their actions as opposed to just being twisted for the sake of being twisted. This is honestly the Comics' essence brought to life and I like it. I really hope to see more. P.S: If you made it this far, Simon Pegg saying "Jings" made my whole entire year.

From what I gather, this isn't just a "what would happen if the Justice League were "evil". Nor is it just a, "what would ACTUALLY happen if superhero's were real". I mean, yet it touches on all those points and it does it in excellent fashion (you bet your ass society would monopolize superheroes). But it's also touching on what North American society does to their celebrities. Homelander: Clearly the religious right. Embodies everything America stands for but is ultimately rotten to it's core. Current America. Translucient: Surveillance. He doesn't really do anything bad. Except for being a peeping Tom. But nobody is stopping him. Domestic surveillance of citizens. Don't worry about it because you're not doing anything bad....except you're still be spied upon. Queen Maeve: Apathy to everything around her. This is supposed to be the American people. Used to be in a relationship with the American Dream (Homelander) but has since lost her way. She does see the upcoming generation as hopeful and gives the new generation a pep talk to not be apathetic. A-Train: How professional athletes are treated in America. You can commit a heinous crime and the media will eat up the apology and move on. It also touches upon the need for celebrity athletes to always be the best in their field. Even if it means it hurts/kills them. Look at A-train like they look at Lance Armstrong. Starlight: The resurgence of old American values. Christian, white, "virgin". She was taken advantage of when she was naive. But now that she's "seen" the world, she's using her voice to make change. Similar to how the #metoo movement help resurge 3rd-wave feminism (more or less equality for all). She's the new American ideals. There to challenge the corrupted American dream to be better. Black Noir: Fuck do I know!? Just my 2 cents after watching this amazing fucking show.

So, for the name of the evil corporation, they wanted a WWII era defense contractor (for vague familiarity), with a checkered past (for context), and that is defunct (for legal reasons). They could have picked “Fairchild”, but no...they had to pick “Vought”, producer of the F-4 Corsair (the gull wing fighter for the Navy). Its bad product? The F-7 Cutlass, the twin jet engine delta wing Navy fighter that had a horrible safety record due to the ridiculously high angle of attack required for takeoffs and landings (because of the very underpowered Allison engines). I work for Vought. Actually, I work for Triumph Aerospace, which purchased the last remnants of Vought Aircraft Industries in 2010. Triumph gradually phased out the name over the next few years, and it only remains with the (stopped) pension plan, and the retirees club (a bunch of old guys who restore old F-4 Corsairs as well as the occasional F-8 Crusader). I hired into LTV (Ling-Temco-Vought) in 1987. I wish I had taken care of the old Vought t-shirts...might be worth something on eBay.

I really liked it! Like, I love a good superhero deconstruction, but they can go into edgelord territory really quickly and the marketing for the show made me think that this would go edgelord. But I saw some good reviews and gave it a chance, and it does well with the concept. It surprised me that they humanized the Supes so much. Like, I thought they'd all just be 100% assholes who are assholes for the sake of being assholes. (again, the marketing seemed pretty edgelord) But we get a lot of moments where we sympathize with the characters, and sometimes even understand why they've done terrible things. And I liked how they managed to make The Deep sympathetic without excusing or toning down what he did to Starlight. A lot of elements in the show are clearly based on the MCU and its mega popularity. Were those elements in the comics? I wouldn't think so, since the comics finished up before the MCU became such a pop culture juggernaut. So assuming it's an adaptational change, I think it's a good one, makes the whole "superhero deconstruction" thing more modern and relevant. And as a big MCU slut, I enjoy those references, lol. I hope we get more of Queen Maeve in the next season. This season made it clear that there's a lot to her character but it doesn't go deep into it.

I really enjoyed the show, it was strong and did great world building. SPOILERS A few complaints, though. The non-ending was too sudden and jarring. It was like being half way through a book, and somebody just yanks it out of your hands midway through reading a sentence, and says you can finish it in two years. That's not suspenseful, that's not a cliffhanger, that's just cutting the story off suddenly when it shouldn't have been. This really needed to either be 12 episodes per season, or find a way to satisfyingly end the storyline in 8. It did neither, and just ended abruptly in a very poorly fashioned way. The last two episodes were definitely the weakest, especially the 7th. Not so much the plot, just the general writing. Some character decisions didn't make much sense, like Annie asking to meet Hughie to hear what he has to say, then suddenly not wanting to hear what he has to say. Butcher coming out of no where and starts shooting her, and hughie just casually jogs over to Butcher instead of seeing if Annie was OK? How did it suddenly escalate to that, and why would he just walk away? It didn't strike me as in-character for any of them. Also, the scene with A-Train and Hughie's father. It ends with her Kimiko just wacking his leg, and then they both just walk away? Why didn't they do something else? It seems like there should have been a second half to that plan. Yes I know the focus was on getting his father out of there, but he has a lot of emotions with A-Train, yet he just walks away and leaves him to recover? It seemed contrived just to get the ending of that character arc in the final episode, in the warehouse. And then there's the episode with Translucent. If you are going to build an entire hour episode up in a way that you are showing characters desperately, with their lives on the line, finding a way to kill somebody with invulnerable skin, maybe don't end with the most obvious answer that I think just about everybody would think of first . Of course they should have tried to go through the fleshy bits. That's the first thought that would pop into everybody's minds. It was the first idea that popped into mine. So it was really disappointing and frustrating to drag that out, and have the characters only think of that last. It wasn't very realistic, and ended up being a big letdown. And lastly, why did The Deep just sit there and let that woman hurt him? There was literally no power, social, physical, coercive, or otherwise the woman had that would allow her the freedom to do what she was doing. They spent hours, the first 3-4 episodes carefully constructing a world showing Supes doing literally anything they want whenever they want, because they are humans, but with extra power and strength. They rape, murder, maim, threaten, and bully for their own amusement. Everybody explicitly understands this. The Deep could have done what any Supe has done a million times before, hell what he himself has done a million times before, and coerce her into silence by mere threat of death. I understand the writers were attempting to both give him his just deserts and show that rape isn't just about physical strength, but those rules are not really the rules of The Boys universe, those are our rules in our universe. Supes literally do whatever they want, and use their strength and powers to get away with it. The Deep had all the cards, so to speak, and she had nothing. She wants to "talk" and claim he raped her? She ends up having an "accident" involving a shark or something. That's the universe of The Boys, and why nobody crosses a Supe. So it was very incongruous with the established universe to have The Deep just sit there and get hurt. It made little sense. But beyond that, it was still a very good show. Very memorable, very engaging and entertaining.

I’m going to be real honest but “The boys” really has me on the ropes, like I could go either way. Personally I’m a huge fan of the comic. The original series, Herogasm, the origin stories all have a place on my shelf and get picked up probably once a year. I realize that I’m probably one of those people that love the comic so much that any changes will seem like sacrilege. On the other hand I only signed up to reddit because I wanted to talk to people about this. So here we are, you all will have to suffer me now ;-) Now here’s what I like about the series: it looks great. Nothing cheap. Nothing half assed. Amazone really spent some money on this. Ennis must be laughing his ass off. After DC cancelling the boys, then it being turned into a really popular series... now that’s what I call Karma. all the supes pretty much look like I imagined they would. They look almost better than in the comics. Really really good job. I appreciate the comic nods: “Do you have a dog?” “petite Hughie” etc. that at least acknowledges that they didn’t “forget” something but it was a choice to change it. I was afraid that I would know everything that’s happening. But they changed it up really nicely and added some lore that I enjoy. Now here’s what I don’t like or at least what I would like to talk about: the whole point of the comic was how dekadent and horrible the supes were. Normal people were like their play things. We were a nuisance and nothing more. I realize that they needed to switch it up a bit but c’mon. Translucent has a kid. The Deep (why is he white? Is that a play on Aquaman?) loves Dolphins? A-Train actually loves  Popclaw etc. I’m at episode 4 and right now the Boys seem like the bad guys. It wasn’t supposed to be like that. The Boys were bad (Butcher might have been evil at some point) but they were NECESSARY. Because everything they did had a reason. Right now it seems like Butcher (who’s nowhere near as badass as in the comics) is just an ass. I don’t really like Hughie that much since they changed him to American but I appreciate the Simon Pegg nod. Hughie in the comics is this really genuine guy who’s being manipulated by Butcher, where in the end Butcher fails. Here he’s like “fuck your Translucent there’s a poster on the wall with spaghetti and god I hate spaghetti.” (It’s a joke I realize he probably has PTSD or something like that) Frenchie isn’t some badass womanizer in the comics but actually and truly insane which makes him one of my favorites. Hi, just binged through the season, here are my thoughts for any who are interested disclaimer, i've never read the comics or known of their existence before hearing about the show really love the premise, gives me Watchmen vibes I don't like the random goofy moments, I feel like they don't fit in with the character of the show and kinda kill immersion also there are a few contrived and illogical moments which I felt did the same for immersion as the above on the whole, I feel the show lacks an identity. it alternates between the goofiness and the darkness without every really settling on either. from what i've read on this sub, the comic itself was a lot darker so maybe they made a deliberate attempt to add these goofy moments to lighten the mood. i dont think they work. linked to the above, at the moment the show seems to lack depth. it's a little bit shallow and lacking in depth, perhaps because it doesnt know what it is so has no direction for depth to be projected from. however, i feel like as the show continues and develops a character, it could definitely gain that depth. i feel that the portrayal of the seven is generally speaking much more interesting than that of the protagonists. Homelander especially can become a wonderfully nuanced villain, with a somewhat sympathetic upbringing. my favourite character in the show, due to being written well and/or the actor doing a great job. the protagonists, on the other hand, all seem like fairly routine and unimaginative tropes. i dont see the same depth with them and find them harder to watch. the season itself didnt really have that much tension or buildup. as in, the entire thing played out at pretty much the same rate. there weren't slower episodes to complement faster episodes. it all seemed to be going at a pretty monotonous pace which, for me at least, made it a bit tedious to watch especially towards the latter episodes. i also felt that there were difficulties in certain scenes in telling a story effectively. like the creators knew what they wanted the audience to feel but the writing or performance wasn't there for that to be communicated effectively to the audience. overall a mixed bag, honestly. i thought at times it was terrific and very interesting, and i thought at times it very bad. i am still interested to see season 2, however, and feel like it's a show that could get better as it establishes itself.

For example: by taking away the powers from all The Boys except Kimiko, they make the gender dynamic entirely lopsided. As a result, effectively, every superpowered male character is portrayed as evil and every superpowered female character is good (or flawed but sympathetic at worst). Take Queen Maeve, who is a completely apathetic alcoholic who engages in MMF threesomes in the source material. In the show, she's more of a beaten-down hero who tried to do the right thing and, as a result, is estranged from her partner. In the comics, she can fly, which makes her arguably as responsible for the plane crash as Homelander is (she flees from the plane on her own, accidentally killing passengers in her wake). In the show, because she can't fly, she merely has to make the reluctant choice to leave with Homelander or die, leaving viewers to feel for her even though she nevertheless makes the "bad" decision. Then there's the subplot involving The Deep, which is largely based on outdated "Aquaman is lame" jokes. It's amusing but an entire season of that wears out its welcome. What I feel they should've done is instead of going into the well-worn girl-power, #MeToo route, they could've taken a Paul Verhoven (Robocop, Starship Troopers) approach to the material. The pretzel twists they have to take to create a useless season finale cliffhanger (yeah she's dead, yeah I saw her die in childbirth, oh wait psych! she's not dead lol)  should've been tossed out in favor of a more faithful retelling of Butcher's wife's fate, which is one of the more memorable scenes in the comics. Ennis' version is far from perfect. But the Amazon adaptation is a homogenized product. It's like comparing punk rock from the 70's to happy, 90's punk-pop covers of "Somewhere Over The Rainbow". It's superficially similar and much more professionally-produced. But meh.
